At 06:40 on the third of March, the duty engineer at the north pumping station logged a drop in line pressure and began the standard inspection sequence. The station, built in 1911 and rebuilt twice since, supplies water to four districts through a network of cast-iron mains, most of them laid before the First World War. The engineer first checked the intake screens, then the settling tanks, then the three vertical pumps on the lower floor. All three pumps were running, but the middle unit was drawing noticeably more current than its sisters, and the vibration meter bolted to its bearing housing showed a reading well above the tolerance printed on the plate. He shut the unit down, isolated it at the main switch, and locked the breaker before opening the inspection hatch.

Inside the housing he found a broken retaining ring lying in the oil sump, together with a quantity of black sludge that had collected over what appeared to be several months. The ring had scored the shaft along roughly a third of its circumference, and metal filings had been carried through the bearing gallery into the discharge pipe. Because the middle pump shares a common header with the eastern pump, the debris had also reached the check valve on that line, which the engineer found partly jammed when he tested it by hand. He photographed the damage, tagged the components, and rang the maintenance supervisor, who asked him to prepare a written report before the end of the shift.

The report was to include a description of the fault, a list of the parts affected, and a recommendation for the repair schedule. The supervisor also wanted a short account of the inspection itself, so that the procedures manual could be updated before the winter audit.

While waiting for the supervisor to call back, the engineer walked the length of the header gallery with a clipboard and recorded the condition of every fitting. The gallery holds forty-two fittings in all, of which nineteen are original to the 1911 installation and the remainder were replaced during the 1978 refurbishment. He noted corrosion on several flanges, a weeping gasket on the western branch, and a cracked support bracket that had been repaired, badly, with a strip of galvanised plate and two bolts. None of these defects was urgent, he decided, but each would need attention before the winter drawdown.

At 09:15 the supervisor arrived with a replacement ring and a portable press. Together they lifted the middle pump back onto its plinth, refitted the bearing, and ran the unit up to speed under observation. The vibration reading settled within tolerance after twenty minutes, and the discharge pressure returned to normal. The engineer completed his report at 11:30, attached the photographs, and placed the damaged ring in an evidence bag for the stores clerk. The station returned to automatic operation at noon.
